name: Vitamin A (Retinol)
advisoryNotes: High doses (>10,000 IU retinol/day) may cause toxicity; teratogenic at very high doses in pregnancy
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin A Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)
safeUsageLevel: Up to 90 mg/day (adult RDA); 500–1000 mg commonly used
advisoryNotes: Doses >2g/day may cause gastrointestinal distress
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin C Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin D3 (Cholecalciferol)
advisoryNotes: Toxicity possible at >4000 IU/day long-term; fat-soluble accumulation risk
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin D Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin D2 (Ergocalciferol)
advisoryNotes: Less potent than D3 at raising serum 25(OH)D
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin D Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin E (Tocopherol)
advisoryNotes: High dose supplementation (>400 IU/day) may increase all-cause mortality risk per meta-analyses; anticoagulant interactions
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin E Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin K1 (Phylloquinone)
advisoryNotes: Interacts with warfarin; patients on anticoagulants should maintain consistent intake
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin K Fact Sheet

name: Vitamin K2 (Menaquinone)
advisoryNotes: NDI notification may be required depending on form and dose; warfarin interaction same as K1
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin K Fact Sheet

name: Niacin (Vitamin B3)
upperIntakeLevel: 35 mg/day (adults) for niacin (nicotinic acid form); niacinamide UL is 35 mg/day from supplements
advisoryNotes: Pharmacological doses (>1g/day nicotinic acid) cause flushing, liver toxicity; OTC claim limits apply

name: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)
advisoryNotes: Peripheral neuropathy reported at chronic doses >200 mg/day
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin B6 Fact Sheet

name: Folate (Folic Acid)
upperIntakeLevel: 1000 mcg DFE/day from folic acid supplements (adults)
safeUsageLevel: 400 mcg DFE/day (adult RDA); 600 mcg in pregnancy
advisoryNotes: High doses may mask B12 deficiency neurological symptoms

name: Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamin)
safeUsageLevel: 2.4 mcg/day (adult RDA); higher intakes generally safe
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Vitamin B12 Fact Sheet

name: Biotin (Vitamin B7)
advisoryNotes: High doses (>5 mg/day) can interfere with thyroid hormone and cardiac troponin laboratory assays (FDA Safety Communication 2017)
regulatoryCitations: FDA 2017 Biotin Lab Interference Safety Communication

name: Pantothenic Acid (Vitamin B5)
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Pantothenic Acid Fact Sheet

name: Calcium
advisoryNotes: Excess calcium supplementation linked to cardiovascular events in some meta-analyses; may interfere with iron/zinc absorption

name: Iron
advisoryNotes: Iron overdose is leading cause of supplement-related poisoning in children; products >30 mg/dose require child-resistant packaging and warning label per 21 CFR 101.17(e)

name: Magnesium
upperIntakeLevel: 350 mg/day from supplements (adults); no UL for food sources
advisoryNotes: Supplemental doses >350 mg/day may cause diarrhea, nausea

name: Zinc
advisoryNotes: Chronic high intake (>50 mg/day) may cause copper deficiency and immune dysfunction

name: Selenium
advisoryNotes: Selenosis (toxicity) may occur at doses >400 mcg/day

name: Copper
advisoryNotes: Wilson's disease patients should avoid supplemental copper

name: Chromium
advisoryNotes: FDA qualified health claim for chromium picolinate and insulin resistance has limited evidence. Hexavalent chromium is a Prop 65 chemical; trivalent form in supplements is different but California warning may still apply at high doses.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Qualified Health Claim Chromium Picolinate

name: Manganese
advisoryNotes: Excessive intake may cause neurological symptoms (manganism)

name: Iodine
advisoryNotes: Thyroid disorders may be exacerbated by excess iodine; kelp sources have variable iodine content

name: Potassium
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL from food; supplement doses >99 mg/serving require medical supervision labeling
advisoryNotes: FDA limits OTC potassium supplements to 99 mg per dose unit. Higher doses require Rx. Risk of cardiac arrhythmia in patients with kidney disease.

name: Boron
advisoryNotes: No RDA established; DSHEA grandfathered but limited FDA guidance

name: Vanadium
safeUsageLevel: No RDA established; use with caution
advisoryNotes: On FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List. Marketed for blood sugar control but FDA has not authorized these claims. Potential toxicity at supplemental doses.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List

name: Melatonin
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; typical doses 0.5–5 mg for sleep
advisoryNotes: NDI notification submitted and accepted. Some products contain inconsistent labeling doses (study found actual content varying from labeled). Not approved as drug in US; sold as dietary supplement.

name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
advisoryNotes: May interact with warfarin; may lower blood pressure

name: Omega-3 Fatty Acids (Fish Oil)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; FDA recommends not exceeding 3g/day from supplements
advisoryNotes: Qualified health claim approved for cardiovascular disease risk reduction. High doses may increase bleeding risk. Possible contamination with PCBs, mercury in low-quality fish oil.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Qualified Health Claim Fish Oil

name: Probiotics (Lactobacillus acidophilus)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; typical doses 1–100 billion CFU/day
advisoryNotes: GRAS self-affirmed for many strains. Immunocompromised patients should consult physician. Strain-specific safety data needed per FDA.

name: Probiotics (Bifidobacterium longum)
advisoryNotes: GRAS self-affirmed. Same immunocompromised precaution as all probiotics.

name: L-Glutamine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; doses up to 40g/day studied in clinical settings
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed for food use. Caution in patients with seizure disorders or those taking anticonvulsants.

name: L-Carnitine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 3g/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May cause fishy body odor at high doses. GRN 000057.

name: Creatine Monohydrate
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 20g/day (loading) and 3–5g/day (maintenance) studied
advisoryNotes: Well-studied. FDA has not objected to GRAS notifications. Some studies used 20g/day loading phases safely. Caution in patients with renal impairment.

name: Caffeine
upperIntakeLevel: 400 mg/day (adults); FDA has issued guidance on pure powdered caffeine
safeUsageLevel: Up to 200 mg/dose; up to 400 mg/day total
advisoryNotes: FDA warned against pure powdered caffeine (extremely concentrated); 1 teaspoon equals ~25 cups of coffee. FDA warning letters issued to companies marketing very high-dose caffeine. Pregnant women advised to limit to <200 mg/day.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Warning Letters on High-Dose Caffeine

name: Beta-Alanine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 6.4g/day studied
advisoryNotes: Paresthesia (tingling sensation) common side effect at doses >800 mg. NDI not required as GRAS self-affirmed.

name: Branched-Chain Amino Acids (BCAAs)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed for individual amino acids. No established UL for BCAAs as a category.

name: Whey Protein
advisoryNotes: Milk allergen — must declare on label per FALCPA (21 CFR 101.4). Heavy metal contamination (lead, cadmium) has been found in some products.

name: Collagen Peptides
advisoryNotes: Potential allergen for fish/shellfish (marine collagen) or bovine-sensitive individuals. Not a complete protein (low tryptophan).

name: Hyaluronic Acid
advisoryNotes: NDI may be required depending on source (bacterial fermentation vs. animal-derived) and intended use. GRN 000255 on file.

name: Glucosamine
advisoryNotes: Shellfish-derived forms must declare shellfish allergen. May affect blood glucose in diabetics.

name: Chondroitin Sulfate
advisoryNotes: Often combined with glucosamine. Possible interaction with warfarin.

name: Turmeric (Curcumin)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 8g/day curcumin studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed for turmeric as spice. Bioavailability enhanced by piperine (black pepper extract) or lipid formulations. High doses may cause GI distress. May interact with anticoagulants.

name: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 1250 mg/day root extract studied
advisoryNotes: GRN 000764 on file. FDA has not objected. Possible thyroid hormone interaction. Avoid in pregnancy. Rare hepatotoxicity cases reported at high doses.

name: Rhodiola Rosea
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered as traditional herb. No FDA objection to current use. May interact with antidepressants (MAO inhibitors).

name: Valerian Root (Valeriana officinalis)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavoring substance. Not recommended during pregnancy. Drowsiness — advise against driving after use.

name: St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum)
safeUsageLevel: 300 mg three times daily (standardized to 0.3% hypericin) studied
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED use — major drug interaction warning. FDA issued public health advisory in 2000. CYP3A4 inducer; significantly reduces blood levels of HIV antiretrovirals, cyclosporin, oral contraceptives, digoxin, warfarin, and many other drugs. Label must warn of drug interactions.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Public Health Advisory 2000 (St. John's Wort)

name: Ginkgo Biloba
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered. May increase bleeding risk; avoid with anticoagulants. Seizure risk at very high doses. NTP studies found carcinogenicity in rodents but not confirmed in humans at typical doses.

name: Saw Palmetto (Serenoa repens)
safeUsageLevel: 160 mg twice daily of standardized extract typical
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered. Widely used for BPH/prostate health. Cannot make disease claims about BPH treatment — only structure/function claims about urinary/prostate health.
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Saw Palmetto Fact Sheet

name: Echinacea
safeUsageLevel: 1–4 g dried herb/day or standardized extract equivalent
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered. Caution in autoimmune conditions. May interact with immunosuppressants. Short-term use (up to 8 weeks) studied.

name: Elderberry (Sambucus nigra)
advisoryNotes: Cooked/processed elderberry is safe; raw elderberries contain cyanogenic glycosides. Immune-stimulating effects may be problematic in autoimmune conditions.

name: Berberine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 2g/day studied
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered (found in goldenseal, barberry). Significant drug interactions via CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibition. May lower blood glucose — caution in diabetics on medication. Not for use in pregnancy (uterine stimulant).

name: Resveratrol
advisoryNotes: NDI notification filed and on file at FDA. No objection received. May interact with anticoagulants at high doses.

name: Green Tea Extract (EGCG)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; hepatotoxicity concern at >800 mg EGCG/day
safeUsageLevel: Up to 338 mg EGCG/day (FDA 2017 limit for fasted intake)
advisoryNotes: FDA issued advisory: concentrated green tea extract supplements have been associated with rare but serious liver injury (hepatotoxicity), particularly when taken on an empty stomach. FDA proposed warning label language in 2020. Products with >800 mg EGCG per day may trigger FDA scrutiny.
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Green Tea Fact Sheet

name: Garcinia Cambogia
safeUsageLevel: Use with caution; liver safety concerns at high doses
advisoryNotes: Multiple FDA warning letters issued to companies making unsupported weight loss claims. Rare cases of liver toxicity reported. Weight loss efficacy evidence is weak. Structure/function claims limited.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Warning Letters on Weight Loss Supplements

name: Bitter Orange (Synephrine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; cardiovascular effects at >50 mg/day
advisoryNotes: On FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List. Commonly used as ephedra substitute after FDA banned ephedrine alkaloids. Multiple adverse event reports involving cardiovascular events. Often combined with caffeine, increasing risk. FDA has issued caution communications.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List

name: Ephedra (Ma Huang)
upperIntakeLevel: BANNED — no safe dose as dietary supplement
advisoryNotes: BANNED by FDA since April 2004 (21 CFR Part 119). Ephedrine alkaloid-containing dietary supplements were found to present unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Final rule published 69 FR 6788. Multiple deaths and cardiovascular events linked. Manufacturing or distribution of ephedrine alkaloid-containing dietary supplements is illegal.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Ban on Ephedra-Containing Dietary Supplements

name: DMAA (1,3-Dimethylamylamine)
upperIntakeLevel: BANNED — not a legal dietary supplement ingredient
advisoryNotes: FDA determined DMAA is not a lawful dietary supplement ingredient. FDA issued multiple warning letters and initiated seizures. Not a natural constituent of geranium oil as some manufacturers claimed. Associated with hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular events. Criminal prosecutions have occurred.

name: DMBA (1,3-Dimethylbutylamine)
advisoryNotes: DMBA (marketed as AMP Citrate) was developed as a DMAA analog after DMAA was banned. FDA issued warning letters stating it does not meet the definition of a dietary supplement ingredient. Products containing DMBA are adulterated.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Warning Letters on DMBA/AMP Citrate 2015

name: Androstenedione
advisoryNotes: Classified as anabolic steroid under the Anabolic Steroid Control Act. FDA warned that androstenedione-containing supplements are illegal. Schedule III controlled substance.

name: Aristolochic Acid
advisoryNotes: FDA banned in 2001. Aristolochic acids are potent nephrotoxins (kidney failure) and human carcinogens. Found as contaminants in some Chinese herbal products. Any product containing Aristolochia species is subject to seizure. FDA advises consumers not to use any product that might contain aristolochic acid.

name: Kava (Piper methysticum)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; liver injury cases at typical doses
safeUsageLevel: Use with caution; short-term use only
advisoryNotes: FDA issued consumer advisory in 2002 about potential liver injury from kava-containing products. Cases of liver failure (including requiring transplantation) reported. Listed on California Prop 65. DSHEA grandfathered but FDA advisory in effect. Not recommended for use beyond 4–8 weeks without medical supervision.

name: Comfrey (Symphytum officinale)
safeUsageLevel: External use only; oral products banned
advisoryNotes: FDA issued statement in 2001 advising companies to remove oral comfrey products from the market. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) which cause veno-occlusive disease and liver damage. Listed on Prop 65. Topical products permitted with pyrrolizidine-free labeling requirements.

name: Yohimbe (Yohimbine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; adverse events at >20 mg/day yohimbine
safeUsageLevel: 5–20 mg/day yohimbine HCl studied; use with caution
advisoryNotes: On FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List. Significant cardiovascular and psychiatric adverse events reported (tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, seizures). Interacts with many medications including MAO inhibitors, antidepressants. FDA has sent warning letters for products making erectile dysfunction drug claims.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List
FDA Warning Letters on Sexual Enhancement Products

name: N-Acetyl Cysteine (NAC)
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — significant legal uncertainty. FDA declared in August 2020 that NAC cannot be lawfully marketed as a dietary supplement because it was first approved as a drug (Mucomyst/acetylcysteine) before being marketed as a supplement. FDA sent warning letters to Amazon and other retailers in 2021. Current legal status under review; FDA announced in 2022 it may reconsider. Companies should seek legal guidance before marketing NAC supplements.

name: Quercetin
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 1g/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavonoid. DSHEA grandfathered. May interact with certain antibiotics (fluoroquinolones) and may affect drug metabolism via CYP enzymes.

name: Spirulina
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May contain heavy metals (arsenic, lead) depending on source — supplier CoA critical. Distinction from cyanobacteria that produce toxins (microcystins) must be maintained through testing.

name: Chlorella
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Heavy metal testing (arsenic, cadmium, lead) required given algal source. Cell wall must be broken for digestibility.

name: Phosphatidylserine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 600 mg/day studied
advisoryNotes: FDA qualified health claim authorized for cognitive function (reduced risk of dementia): very limited evidence. Claim must be phrased carefully per FDA guidance.

name: Alpha-Lipoic Acid (ALA)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 1200 mg/day studied
advisoryNotes: NDI notification submitted to FDA; no objection received. May lower blood glucose — caution in diabetics on medication. Possible thiamine (B1) depletion at high doses.

name: 5-HTP (5-Hydroxytryptophan)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; toxicity concerns at high doses
advisoryNotes: NDI notification on file. Serotonin syndrome risk when combined with SSRIs, MAOIs, or other serotonergic agents — this is a significant drug interaction requiring a warning label. Do not combine with antidepressant medications.

name: GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid)
advisoryNotes: NDI notification filed; GRAS notification submitted (GRN pending). Oral bioavailability to the brain is debated. Generally considered safe at typical doses.

name: Maca Root (Lepidium meyenii)
advisoryNotes: GRN filed for maca root. Generally recognized as safe at food-level use. Should not be used in patients with hormone-sensitive conditions (contains glucosinolates that may affect thyroid).

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom (Hericium erinaceus)
advisoryNotes: GRAS notification filed. Generally safe in short-term studies. Possible allergen for individuals allergic to mushrooms.

name: Reishi Mushroom (Ganoderma lucidum)
safeUsageLevel: 1.5–9 g/day of dried powder or extract equivalent
advisoryNotes: NDI notification may be required for high-potency extracts. DSHEA grandfathered for whole mushroom forms. May interact with anticoagulants.

name: Cordyceps (Cordyceps sinensis / militaris)
advisoryNotes: NDI notification may be required for concentrated extracts. Generally tolerated. May interact with immunosuppressants and blood thinners.

name: Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus)
safeUsageLevel: 9–15 g dried root/day traditional; 250–500 mg extract typical
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered. May interact with immunosuppressants. Adulteration with Astragalus species containing toxic alkaloids has been documented.

name: Holy Basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavoring. DSHEA grandfathered. May lower blood glucose and blood pressure.

name: Bacopa monnieri
advisoryNotes: NDI notification may be required for concentrated extracts. Generally tolerated; may cause GI distress. Cognitive benefits studied over ≥12 weeks.

name: Acetyl-L-Carnitine (ALCAR)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 3g/day studied
advisoryNotes: NDI notification on file. Different from L-Carnitine; crosses blood-brain barrier. Generally well tolerated.

name: L-Theanine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 900 mg/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS notification GRN 000209 on file; no objection. Generally recognized as safe. Often combined with caffeine for focus/alertness.

name: Citrulline Malate
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 15g/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS notification filed. Precursor to arginine. Commonly used in pre-workout formulations.

name: Arginine (L-Arginine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 30g/day studied in clinical settings
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May exacerbate herpes simplex outbreaks at high doses. Possible interaction with blood pressure medications.

name: Taurine
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 6g/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as a food ingredient. Commonly used in energy drinks and pre-workout supplements.

name: Tyrosine (L-Tyrosine)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Caution in patients taking MAO inhibitors, thyroid medications, or levodopa.

name: Phenylalanine (L-Phenylalanine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL for healthy individuals
safeUsageLevel: Typical dietary amounts safe for most individuals
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — required labeling: products containing phenylalanine must include 'Contains Phenylalanine' warning per 21 CFR 101.21. Individuals with PKU (phenylketonuria) cannot metabolize phenylalanine and must strictly avoid it. Applies to all food and supplement products.

name: Inositol
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 18g/day studied for OCD
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Commonly used for PCOS, mental health support. Bipolar patients should consult physician.

name: Digestive Enzymes (Bromelain)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Pineapple allergy precaution. May enhance antibiotic absorption. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.

name: Digestive Enzymes (Papain)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Latex-fruit syndrome possible in latex-allergic individuals.

name: Betaine (Trimethylglycine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 20g/day studied clinically
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Betaine HCl (for stomach acid support) should be taken with meals to avoid esophageal irritation.

name: Milk Thistle (Silymarin)
advisoryNotes: DSHEA grandfathered. Well-studied liver protectant herb. May interact with P450 enzymes; possible interaction with indinavir and other CYP3A4 substrates.
regulatoryCitations: NIH ODS Milk Thistle Fact Sheet

name: Black Pepper Extract (Piperine)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; typical supplement dose 5–20 mg
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as spice extract. Enhances bioavailability of many nutrients including curcumin. May increase absorption of pharmaceuticals — warn patients on medications.

name: Ginger Root (Zingiber officinale)
safeUsageLevel: 250–2000 mg/day dried root or equivalent extract
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May inhibit platelet aggregation at high doses — caution with anticoagulants.

name: Garlic (Allium sativum)
safeUsageLevel: 600–1200 mg/day dried garlic or equivalent AGE
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May have mild antiplatelet and blood pressure lowering effects. FDA qualified health claim for reduction of cardiovascular risk is not approved (insufficient evidence).

name: Red Yeast Rice
upperIntakeLevel: N/A — contains lovastatin (controlled substance level dependent)
safeUsageLevel: Subject to FDA enforcement if monacolin K content is significant
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — complex legal status. Red yeast rice containing monacolin K (identical to lovastatin, an FDA-approved drug) is considered an unauthorized drug by FDA. FDA has issued multiple warning letters and import alerts. Products standardized to contain monacolin K are adulterated/misbranded. Low-monacolin RYR may be marketed as supplement but this distinction is difficult to enforce. Buyers should be cautious.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Warning Letters on Red Yeast Rice

name: Probiotic (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed for this specific strain. Well-studied probiotic. Standard immunocompromised-patient precaution applies.

name: Probiotic (Saccharomyces boulardii)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. Yeast-based probiotic; antifungals (fluconazole) reduce its efficacy. Serious infections possible in immunocompromised patients (fungemia).

name: Prebiotic (Inulin)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; GI tolerance limit ~20–30 g/day
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. FDA allows labeling as dietary fiber. GI distress (bloating, gas) at high doses.

name: MCT Oil (Medium Chain Triglycerides)
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; GI tolerance limit at high doses
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed for food use. GI distress at high doses initially; tolerance develops. High caloric density.

name: Apple Cider Vinegar
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; dental enamel damage at high liquid doses
advisoryNotes: GRAS as vinegar. Liquid form can damage tooth enamel and esophagus if consumed undiluted. Low pH may affect potassium levels at high doses. Some diabetes claims are unsubstantiated.

name: Lemon Balm (Melissa officinalis)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavoring. DSHEA grandfathered. May potentiate sedatives. Possible thyroid effects in large doses (inhibits TSH binding).

name: Passionflower (Passiflora incarnata)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavoring. Not for use in pregnancy. May potentiate CNS depressants.

name: Hormone DHEA (Dehydroepiandrosterone)
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — complicated status. DHEA is grandfathered under DSHEA but is a steroid hormone precursor. FDA declared DHEA as a dietary supplement ingredient (not a drug) in 1996. However, products with drug claims (treating hypoactive sexual desire disorder — only FDA approved Intrarosa Rx) are illegal. Not for use in individuals with hormone-sensitive cancers. May cause androgenic side effects in women.

name: Pregnenolone
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — pregnenolone is a steroid hormone precursor. Status as dietary supplement is contested. FDA has issued warning letters to companies making disease claims. Avoid in hormone-sensitive conditions.

name: Lycopene
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed (GRN 000000 series). FDA rejected qualified health claim for lycopene and prostate/cancer risk as insufficient evidence. Skin discoloration (lycopenodermia) possible at very high doses.
regulatoryCitations: FDA Rejected Qualified Health Claim on Lycopene

name: Lutein
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 20 mg/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed (GRN 000000 series). Used in eye health supplements. Combined with zeaxanthin for macular health.

name: Zeaxanthin
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. NDI notification filed. Commonly paired with lutein for eye health.

name: Astaxanthin
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL; up to 40 mg/day studied
advisoryNotes: GRAS notification filed (GRN 000000 series). NDI notification on file. May have mild blood-thinning effect at high doses.

name: Colostrum
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as dairy-derived ingredient. Milk allergen — must declare. BSE (mad cow disease) risk mitigation: must be sourced from USDA-inspected dairy cattle.

name: Pea Protein
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed. May not be a 'complete' protein (lower methionine). Heavy metal contamination testing recommended.

name: Hemp Protein / Hemp Seeds
upperIntakeLevel: No established UL for hemp seeds/protein
safeUsageLevel: Dietary use consistent with food-level intake
advisoryNotes: Hemp seed (hulled) and hemp seed oil/protein from the mature stalk/seeds are legal under the 2018 Farm Bill (THC <0.3%). GRAS notification pending for hemp seed protein. Distinct from CBD (which has different regulatory status). Labeling must not create confusion with marijuana.

name: CBD (Cannabidiol)
upperIntakeLevel: N/A — not approved as dietary supplement
safeUsageLevel: Legal status as supplement is unresolved
advisoryNotes: RESTRICTED — CBD is NOT approved as a dietary supplement ingredient under current FDA policy (as of 2024). FDA has stated that CBD was approved as a drug (Epidiolex) before it could be marketed as a dietary supplement, triggering 21 USC 321(ff)(3)(B)(ii). FDA has issued hundreds of warning letters to CBD supplement companies. Congress has considered legislation to change this status. Companies marketing CBD supplements face significant legal risk. California Prop 65 warning may be required.

name: Elderflower (Sambucus nigra flowers)
advisoryNotes: GRAS affirmed as flavoring substance. Flowers and ripe berries are safe; other parts of the plant contain cyanogenic glycosides.

name: Lutein Esters
advisoryNotes: GRAS notification on file. NDI filed for concentrated forms. Must declare lutein ester content vs. free lutein on label.
